extractionNotes: FULL EXTRACTION COMPLETE (all 3 years, all 4 strands, all 10 sub-strands x 3 years = 30 sub-strand-year blocks) verified by direct count against this file's own content: 57 Learning Outcomes and 36 Content Standards, matching the Scope-and-Sequence 'Overall Totals (SHS 1-3)' EXACTLY (CS 36, LO 57). Learning Indicators total 102 in this file versus 105 in the Scope-and-Sequence summary table; per the Extraction feasibility note (that summary table's numeric columns extract badly garbled/run-together, e.g. '5112124'), and since every individual Sub-Strand/Content Standard's Learning Indicators were counted directly and completely from the body content tables (no LI codes skipped within any Content Standard observed), this 3-LI shortfall relative to 105 is attributed to the summary table itself being unreliable rather than to missed content; recorded here rather than silently reconciled. Year-by-year LI subtotals as extracted: Year 1 = 40, Year 2 = 32, Year 3 = 30.

STRUCTURAL DEVIATION FROM CANONICAL SCHEMA: this document's Scope-and-Sequence table reports Overall Totals (SHS 1-3): Content Standards 36, Learning Outcomes 57, Learning Indicators 105 -- i.e. more Learning Outcomes than Content Standards (57 vs 36), the opposite ordering assumed by the canonical schema's per-Learning-Outcome nesting of contentStandards (which assumes CS<=LO per LO or 1:1). Direct in-body verification (e.g. Year 1 Sub-Strand 'Engineering in Society' has 2 Learning Outcomes -- 1.1.1.LO.1, 1.1.1.LO.2 -- but only ONE Content Standard, 1.1.1.CS.1, shared by both) confirms the source presents Learning Outcomes and Content Standards as two SEPARATE tables per Sub-Strand block, without an explicit LO-to-CS mapping line/reference. To avoid fabricating a mapping or duplicating Content Standard/Learning Indicator content under multiple Learning Outcomes, this file stores 'learningOutcomes' and 'contentStandards' as SIBLING arrays directly under each subStrand object (contentStandards is NOT nested inside a learningOutcome here), each contentStandards[].learningIndicators nested as in the canonical schema. This is the 'subject-specific extension point' anticipated by docs/curriculum-extraction-schema.md Phase 5 design notes. Every subStrand-year block's true LO/CS/LI counts were verified by direct count against body content and cross-checked against the Scope-and-Sequence table's Year-1 column total (CS=11, LO=21) which matches exactly.

Scope-and-Sequence summary table (PDF printed page 21, pdfPageIndex 23) extracts with numeric columns badly run together/garbled (e.g. '5112124', '41 13 18 34 12 18 30') due to dense multi-column layout, exactly as flagged in the prior inventory pass. This file's Strand/Sub-Strand totals and all LO/CS/LI/AS records are taken from direct extraction of the body content tables (verified page by page), which extract with good fidelity and are treated as authoritative over the garbled summary table, per task instructions.

A recurring stray extraction artifact appears at multiple points in the raw text layer: an unreadable glyph/icon sequence resembling "'^Z/Z" / "^ZZZZ>" (e.g. adjacent to 1.1.1.LO.2's row on printed page 22-23, and again adjacent to 2.1.1.LO.1's row on printed page 68). This is almost certainly a decorative icon/image element in the page margin that pdftotext -layout cannot render as text and folds into the stream as garbage glyphs; it is not curriculum content. Preserved verbatim only where noted in a reviewNote on the affected Learning Outcome, since its position raises the possibility that it is obscuring/replacing an actual word (see 1.1.1.LO.2 reviewNote).

A one-off character-doubling extraction artifact renders the 'Teaching and Learning Resources' header as 'Teeaacchhiinnggaanndd Learning RReessoouurrcceess' at the end of Sub-Strand 3.1 'Engineering Design' (Year 1, printed page 49-50). This is a font/encoding rendering artifact (the identical header renders correctly as 'Teaching and Learning Resources' everywhere else in the document) rather than genuine document content; normalised to 'Teaching and Learning Resources' in this file's header field per the extraction-tooling-artifact-vs-content distinction used in the Biomedical Science precedent (Þ ligature normalisation), and noted here rather than per-node.

Page numbering: pdftotext page index (pdfPageIndex, 1-based raw PDF page count) is consistently 2 greater than the printed footer/header page number seen in the body text for every page checked in this document (e.g. pdfPageIndex 24 prints 'ENGINEERING | 23'/'22 | ENGINEERING'; pdfPageIndex 143 prints 'ENGINEERING | 141'). Applied throughout this file as pdfPageIndex = printed page + 2.

Bullet sub-items printed under a labelled skill/value category (e.g. 'Communication: o Learners hone... o Learners develop...') are preserved verbatim as 'o '-prefixed segments concatenated into the single guidance string field, rather than split into a separate array, to match the canonical schema's string-typed twentyFirstCenturySkills/gesi fields while keeping the bullet structure visible.

Multi-column Teaching and Learning Resources bullet grids (2 columns per Sub-Strand block) are reconstructed in row-major reading order (left column item, right column item, next row...) exactly as printed, following the same conservative approach used for Biomedical Science's TLR grids.

Front matter (PDF pages 1-21, printed pages 1-19) is the same generic shared SHS boilerplate (SHS Curriculum Overview, Philosophy/Vision/Goal/Rationale of Engineering, 21st Century Skills, GESI, SEL, Learning and Teaching Approaches, UDL, Bloom's/Webb's DoK framework, Curriculum Development Panel list, Scope-and-Sequence table) -- not re-extracted per-node, per the schema's Phase 5 design notes (document-level context, not curriculum-tree content).

SCHEMA-NORMALIZATION PASS (2026-09-29): re-nested this file's sibling-level `contentStandards` arrays (documented in the STRUCTURAL DEVIATION note above) into each subStrand's learningOutcomes[].contentStandards, matching the canonical shape used by every other subject file (contentStandards nested inside its owning learningOutcome). Applied the same CS-covers-multiple-LO convention already established in additional-mathematics.json and english-language.json: in every subStrand where a single Content Standard is shared by multiple sibling Learning Outcomes, the Content Standard was nested under its closest topical-match Learning Outcome (a reviewNote on that Content Standard documents which sibling Learning Indicators map to which other Learning Outcome's topic), and every orphaned sibling Learning Outcome was given an empty contentStandards array plus a reviewNote cross-referencing the Learning Outcome that now holds the shared Content Standard, with extractionStatus set to NEEDS_REVIEW. Since every Content Standard code shares its full subStrand-level prefix with all of that subStrand's Learning Outcome codes (e.g. CS "1.1.1.CS.1" vs LO "1.1.1.LO.1"/"1.1.1.LO.2"), code-prefix matching alone could never disambiguate which specific Learning Outcome a Content Standard belongs to within this file; every assignment therefore required reading Content Standard/Learning Indicator descriptions against Learning Outcome descriptions. 20 of this file's 30 subStrands (holding 20 of the file's 36 Content Standards) had more Learning Outcomes than Content Standards and required genuine topical judgment among multiple plausible candidate Learning Outcomes to decide which one hosts the shared Content Standard — these are listed in this file's Content Standard reviewNote fields for prefixes 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 1.1.3, 2.1.2, 2.1.3, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 2.2.3, 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.3, 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 1.4.2 (Content Standard 1.4.2.CS.1 only), and 3.4.1. The hardest of these was 3.2.2 (Renewable Energy Systems, SHS 3), whose two Learning Outcomes are worded almost identically ("explain wind and bioenergy systems" vs "explain the architecture of wind and bioenergy systems"), making the LI-to-LO topical boundary unusually soft. Sub-Strand 1.4.2 (Embedded Systems, SHS 1) was the only subStrand with more than 2 Learning Outcomes sharing Content Standards (4 LOs / 2 CS): Content Standard 1.4.2.CS.1 required judgment (its Learning Indicators span 3 sibling Learning Outcomes' topics), while 1.4.2.CS.2 (the Arduino Platform) mapped cleanly and unambiguously onto Learning Outcome 1.4.2.LO.4 by content alone despite the shared code prefix. The remaining 10 subStrands had an equal count of Learning Outcomes and Content Standards (five 1-LO/1-CS subStrands, trivially 1:1; five 2-LO/2-CS subStrands — 2.3.1, 2.3.2, 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 2.4.2 — where sequential Content-Standard-to-Learning-Outcome order was confirmed unambiguous by content, e.g. 2.3.1.CS.1 "select an optimal solution" matches 2.3.1.LO.1 "select the most suitable solution" and 2.3.1.CS.2 "design and build working prototypes" matches 2.3.1.LO.2 "design prototypes"), so those 16 Content Standard assignments needed no ambiguity resolution beyond a single confirming read. No content-standard descriptions, learning indicators, guidance text, codes, sources, or pre-existing NEEDS_REVIEW flags were altered by this pass — only the nesting location changed, plus the new reviewNote/extractionStatus fields documented above. Validated post-pass: subStrand (30), learningOutcome (57), contentStandard (36) and learningIndicator (102) counts are byte-for-byte unchanged from the pre-pass totals, and the file re-parses as valid JSON.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate an understanding of the place of engineering in societal development.

learningIndicators.description: Classify the various engineering occupational disciplines.
pedagogicalExemplars: Managing Talk for Learning: In a moderated discussion, learners share their understanding of (a) who an engineer is and (b) what engineering entails. Learners should further describe the work of any engineers they know and explain how important they perceive their work. Furthermore, learners should describe any engineering works they have seen in their communities, on television or through other media.

Initiating Talk for Learning: The Facilitator introduces the various disciplines in engineering, starting with those that were previously mentioned by learners. For each discipline introduced, individual learners should discuss their role in national development. Use webbing or mind maps to organise learners' thoughts.
Experiential Learning: Learners watch videos about engineers performing various tasks and discuss their observations. Organise learners' observations with board summaries

Each group should elect a representative to present the thoughts of the group to the class.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate ability to characterise general industrial automation control devices and implement simple automated systems.

learningIndicators.description: Design and implement simple industrial automated systems using a combination of motors, fluid power systems, sensors and actuators, switches and relays based on design requirements
pedagogicalExemplars: Talk for Learning: The facilitator provides basic theory in the area of motor starter and control circuits, contactors and relays, switches, fluid power systems, sensors and PLCs and how they are integrated for industrial control. Learners are also introduced to the ladder programming language for PLCs.

Experiential Learning: Field Trip: Learners take a trip to a factory or site with a PLC-based industrial automation system in place and observe the roles of the various components, such as motors, sensors, contactors, relays, and fluid power systems in the respective installation, taking note of the engineering diagrams and other documentation for the site. Learners could also tour the industrial automation laboratory for a similar experience.

Project-based hands-on sessions: Learners are taken through simple concepts of industrial automation using simple PLC-based projects such as an Automated door opening system, an Automated room light controller with a bi-directional visitor counter, an Elevator controller, a Water pumping controller, etc. The learners begin with connecting components within the respective projects according to diagrams and downloading programmes onto the PLCs interfaced with the hardware for control. The facilitator explains the function of each component and code (in the case of ladder programming) in the respective project and leaves learners to further explore by manipulating components and observing system behaviour. In some projects, the facilitator may start with the simplest version of the implementation and move through the modifications systematically with the learners to gradually introduce more complex functions or features.
Guest Speaker: Inviting automation engineers to share experiences with learners will enhance the learning experience and make it more relevant.

Self-Directed Learning: Explore online resources: There are many online resources available that can help Learners learn more about PLC programming and automation. Some good options include online tutorials, instructional videos, and forums where learners can ask questions and get feedback from experts. Learners learn additional knowledge and experiences of PLC-based industrial control and present individual reports.

Project-based Experiential Learning: Incorporate hands-on projects that allow learners to apply their CAD skills to real-world design challenges. This can help them develop their problem-solving skills and better understand the design process.
